    "additionalContext": "<EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT>
You are running drovr — a single-writer, clean-context working discipline. It is your default operating mode.

**Below is the full content of your 'drovr:using-drovr' skill — the router that picks the right methodology for the task in front of you and tells you when to escalate into a fresh phase. For all other skills, use the 'Skill' tool:**

---
name: using-drovr
description: Use at the start of every session and before every response, including before clarifying questions and before reading any file — routes to the right drovr skill and requires invoking it whenever there is even a 1% chance one applies
---

**The 1% rule.** If there is even a 1% chance a drovr:* skill applies to what you
are about to do, invoke it. You do not have to be sure: if it turns out not to fit,
say so in a line and drop it, because invoking costs almost nothing. Skipping one
costs the discipline, silently.

**Every turn, not only the first** — before *any* response, including clarifying
questions and read-only exploration. Reading a file to decide what to do is already
doing the task, and mid-task is where this gets skipped.

# Using Drovr

<SUBAGENT-STOP>
If you were dispatched as a subagent to execute a specific task, ignore this
reflex — it is for the human-facing agent, not for you. Do your task.
</SUBAGENT-STOP>

## What this is

Your **always-on router**. Drovr is a working **discipline** and your default
operating mode: this skill does not do the work — it says *how* to work, and
*when* a task has outgrown one context and must become its own phase.

Why: model output degrades as a context window fills (Chroma's *context rot*,
trychroma.com/research/context-rot). A fresh, tight context beats a long one.

## Instruction priority — the human outranks this file

1. **The human's explicit instructions** — what they tell you directly, and what
   `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md` say for them. Highest.
2. **drovr skills** — these outrank your defaults wherever the two disagree.
3. **Your own default behaviour** — lowest.

**Not optional.** Every MUST in drovr is aimed at your defaults, never at the person
you work with. If they tell you to skip a skill, skip it: say once,
plainly, that you are setting it aside because they asked, and get on with their
work.

## The gate

```dot
digraph drovr_gate {
  rankdir=TB;
  node [shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=white];

  msg [label="message received"];
  any [label="does any drovr:* skill apply?\n1% is enough", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  inv [label="invoke it (Skill tool)"];
  say [label="announce it:\n\"Using drovr:<skill> — <purpose>.\""];
  chk [label="numbered checklist\nin the skill?", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  trk [label="one tracked item per step,\nbefore you start step 1"];
  fol [label="follow it"];
  rsp [label="only now: respond", fillcolor=palegreen];

  msg -> any;
  any -> inv [label="yes, or you cannot rule it out"];
  any -> rsp [label="no — silent unless you\ndropped a candidate"];
  inv -> say; say -> chk;
  chk -> trk [label="yes"]; chk -> fol [label="no"];
  trk -> fol; fol -> rsp;
}
```

**The *no* edge is silent by default.** Set a candidate aside? Name it in a clause;
unsaid, it is indistinguishable from never checking. The *yes* announcement stays
mandatory: boilerplate is what dulls it. Silence is for an empty turn, not a borderline
one — at 1% you invoke.

**The checklist branch binds, in full:**

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

## Red flags — you are about to route nothing

Drovr's failure mode is invoking no skill at all and never noticing — nothing goes
wrong at the moment you skip. Catch these before you answer.

| You are thinking | What it is, and what to do |
|---|---|
| *"I already know the shape of it."* · *"I'm fairly sure how this works."* | Familiarity is the trigger, not the exemption — a hunch from an earlier read is not knowing. Invoke the skill that governs finding out. |
| *"I'll just do it quietly, as the first step of the fix."* | You have already decided a methodology applies. Doing it silently drops the invocation, the announcement and the tracked checklist — the three things that make it hold under pressure. Invoke it. |
| *"Announcing which methodology I am following would read as process theatre."* | Announce it in the working record — this session — not the customer-facing thread. That answers the objection; it is not a reason to skip. One sentence, not a speech. |
| *"That is my call to make, not theirs."* · *"Asking just burns clock."* | That settles *who answers*, not *whether a skill applies*. Run the gate before you ask a clarifying question, and before you decide not to ask one. |

## The principle (always)

**Single writer, read-only explorers.** One agent edits at a time. Fan-out
investigation goes to read-only explorers (e.g. `explore-mcp`), never to parallel
writers. This holds whether you stay inline or escalate to phases.

**Always review.** Any change you write gets reviewed before you call it done —
invoke **`drovr:code-review`**; they find, you fix. This is not optional and not
gated on size; it runs inline or across phases, and inline needs no run
(`--base <rev>`). Invoke the skill and let it tell you how to dispatch — never
skip it on a guess about what it will ask for.

## For the task in front of you, apply the right methodology skill

Pick by what you are doing — invoke it via the `Skill` tool before you act:

- Implementing a feature or bugfix → **`drovr:tdd`** (test-first, watch it fail).
- Chasing a bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior → **`drovr:systematic-debugging`**.
- About to claim something is done/fixed/passing → **`drovr:verification-before-completion`**.
- Reviewing an artifact (code, spec, plan) → **`drovr:code-review`**. Per the
  *Always review* rule above, this runs on every change — not only before shipping.

## Escalation contract — inline first

**Default: do the work inline in this session.** Do not reach for phases for a
task that fits. Escalate only when a single context cannot hold the work well.

- **Primary signal — context fullness.** If the transcript is filling to the
  point where output would rot, escalate.
- **Secondary heuristic** (a proxy for the above, not a hard rule): roughly
  **10+ files** touched, or **3+ independent work items**.

When you must escalate, pick the smallest tool that fits:

- **Mid-flight escape hatch — author a HANDOFF yourself.** You are deep in a task
  and this context is filling. You have the whole session in context, so compress
  it *yourself*: write a `HANDOFF.md` (the 7-section shape from `drovr:handoff`,
  git pointers included), then continue in a fresh agent seeded from it. Nothing
  compresses it for you — the finishing agent always authors its own handoff.
- **A single planned boundary → `drovr:handoff`.** Hand finished work across one
  phase boundary to a fresh clean-context agent.
- **A full gated run → `drovr:pipeline`.** Brainstorm → plan → implement → review
  with a human approval gate on `spec.md` before any code is written.

**Putting *any* spec/design in front of a human for approval — even a one-off, not a
full pipeline — goes through the review gate, and the gate has two halves you must run
together:** `drovr review summary <run> "<what changed>"` to present `spec.md`, **and** a
backgrounded `drovr review wait <run>` — the *watch*. `summary` opens the gate and prints
the reviewer's page URL plus the exact watch command; it does **not** start the watch.
Without the watch you never learn the decision and fall back to hand-polling `GET /state`
(the anti-pattern). Revise loop: edit `spec.md` → `review summary` again → re-background
the watch. Exit codes, the state machine and the gotchas live in `drovr:pipeline` → "The
spec gate" — read them there, not from a second copy here that can drift out of step.

**REQUIRED BACKGROUND:** the downstream skills assume this file's contracts —
single-writer rule, the run dir at `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<name>/`, and that
`drovr phase start` spawns `claude` and does **not** inject the seed
(injecting the briefing is the skill's job, via `drovr phase send`).
</EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT>",
    "hookEventName": "SessionStart"
  }
}

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-simplifier:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude.ai Linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

## claude.ai Notion
When query_multiple_data_sources requires the full version of Notion MCP, call notion-show-advanced-analysis-next-steps exactly once after all tool attempts are complete, with no arguments. Do not call the presentation tool again if it has already been called in this turn. The card links to information about full Notion MCP access and the next step available to the caller; it is not a direct checkout or upgrade flow. The renderer returns the card data, including the destination link. Also give the user the relevant next-step message and destination link in the final response. Use a compact, labeled Markdown link rather than a bare URL, and do not request or create a separate link preview. If the renderer is unavailable, rejected, or fails before returning a result, use the full-version message and recovery link from the earlier query_multiple_data_sources result.

## datadog
This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). Consult Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. When the user asks to visualize, chart, or graph data — or when loading a data domain skill (e.g. datadog/traces, datadog/logs, datadog/metrics) — also load datadog/visualizations. Investigation results often benefit from charts.

- agy-review: Use when the user asks for an "agy review", a "gemini review", a second-opinion / adversarial review of the current changes from Gemini, or to run the local Antigravity (`agy`) CLI over a diff. Runs a panel of independent Gemini reviewers (correctness, security, error-handling, type-design) plus a verify pass over the diff, then renders the merged findings as inline notes in the Hunk viewer (via an `--agent-context` sidecar). NOT for in-harness review (use /code-review for that) — this deliberately sends the diff to the user's own Google/Gemini account.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- grill-me: Interview the user relentlessly about a plan or design until reaching shared understanding, resolving each branch of the decision tree. Use when user wants to stress-test a plan, get grilled on their design, or mentions "grill me".
- hunk-review: Interacts with live Hunk diff review sessions via CLI. Inspects review focus, navigates files and hunks, reloads session contents, and adds inline review comments. Use when the user has a Hunk session running or wants to review diffs interactively.
- improve-codebase-architecture: Explore a codebase to find opportunities for architectural improvement, focusing on making the codebase more testable by deepening shallow modules. Use when user wants to improve architecture, find refactoring opportunities, consolidate tightly-coupled modules, or make a codebase more AI-navigable.
- linear-flow: Use in work repos (github.com/modular, modularml, bentoml) BEFORE responding to any of: substantive work ("help me X", "can you X", "add/create/implement/update/replace/fix Y"), brainstorming / design / planning ("let's brainstorm", "let's design", "let's think about", "let's plan", "how should we", "what do you think about", "what would it take to", "what are our options for", "should we"), explicit Linear mentions ("linear", "the ticket", "the issue", or an issue ID like MOD-1234), or `gh pr create`. ALSO fire BEFORE invoking any planning/design/spec skill — most notably the `brainstorming` skill from the superpowers plugin, but also `writing-plans`, `writing-specs`, or any equivalent. The skill must fire BEFORE the agent starts thinking through the problem — brainstorming first and tracking later is a footgun, because by the time a ticket gets filed the agent has already done unscoped work. Tracks the current Linear issue per Claude session in `~/.claude/linear-sessions/`, suggests existing issues or creates new ones, and injects Linear references into PR bodies with closing vs. non-closing magic words. Skips personal repos (dotfiles, hyprland, emacs, AUR), status-only queries, and quick one-off commands.
- nsys-profile: Profile MAX Serve with NVIDIA Nsight Systems. Launches server with deferred profiling, runs benchmark with --trace to capture nsys profile, and prints stats.
- nsys-profile-k8s: Profile a GPU workload on a Kubernetes node using nsys. Deploys a privileged profiling Pod on the same node as the target, captures a trace, and copies it back locally.
- review-until-clean: Use when the user asks to "review in a loop", "iterate until reviewed clean", "review and resolve until clean twice", or any variant that asks for review→fix cycles to a stable end. Spawns a review subagent that runs the simplify and review skills in series, applies issues, re-reviews — terminates only after TWO consecutive clean reports, then auto-commits and pushes.
- tdd: Use this skill whenever the user wants to write code using TDD, test-driven development, or test-first methodology. Triggers on: "/tdd", "let's do TDD", "write a failing test", "red green refactor", "test-first", "start a TDD cycle", or any request to implement a feature by writing tests before code. Adaptive five-step cycle (RED-DOMAIN-GREEN-DOMAIN-COMMIT) that detects harness capabilities and routes to guided (/tdd red|domain|green|commit) or automated (/tdd) mode. NOT for running existing tests, debugging test failures, or reviewing code -- only for the disciplined test-first cycle.
- upgrade-kadabra-rc: Use when cutting/rolling a new kadabra RC for MiniMax-M3, OR whenever the user asks to update/roll/bump the internal deployment or internal endpoint, watch a modular GitHub Actions image build and then update a deployment, update the MAX serve image, roll M3 to a new build, or deploy the new kadabra/max-internal image. Note: the user often calls this just "the internal deployment"/"the internal endpoint" or frames it as "watch the image build and update the deployment" WITHOUT saying kadabra/minimax/RC — this skill still applies. It tags an RC on max/kadabra-release, builds the internal max-internal image via buildAndPushMAXServeImage, bumps the preview (internal, minimax-org minimax-mxfp8-preview) then customer (minimax-org minimax-m3-mxfp8) MiniMax-M3 endpoints with deployment bump, un-sticks the B200 rollout, and verifies (endpoint regression suite, MiniMax Provider Verifier, llm-fuzz) with failing-request monitoring. Keywords: kadabra, RC, minimax, MiniMax-M3, M3, internal deployment, internal endpoint, preview endpoint, bump, roll, deployment bump, max-internal image, image build, MAX serve, watch the image build, update the deployment, roll M3 to the new build, deploy the new kadabra image.
- explain-diff: Use when the user asks for a rich explanation of a code change, diff, branch, or PR.
- review-diff: Use when the user wants a rich, annotated review of a code change, diff, branch, or PR — the diff itself organized, annotated, and shown with surrounding codebase context. Complements explain-diff (which teaches); this one is for reviewing.
- ralph-loop:cancel-ralph: Cancel active Ralph Loop
- ralph-loop:help: Explain Ralph Loop plugin and available commands
- ralph-loop:ralph-loop: Start Ralph Loop in current session
- slack:channel-digest: Get a digest of recent activity across multiple Slack channels
- slack:draft-announcement: Draft a well-formatted Slack announcement and save it as a draft
- slack:find-discussions: Find discussions about a specific topic across Slack channels
- slack:standup: Generate a standup update based on your recent Slack activity
- slack:summarize-channel: Summarize recent activity in a Slack channel
- drovr:code-review: Use when you have written any change, before calling it done or handing it forward — including when you are about to review it by some other means, or to ask a human to authorize a reviewer; requires `drovr code-review run` in the foreground, with every Critical and Important finding resolved or explicitly recorded as deferred

Based on the search results, here's information about configuring Svalboard layout with Vial keymap .vil files:

## Overview
Vial is an open-source cross-platform (Windows, Linux and Mac) GUI and a QMK fork for configuring your keyboard in real time.

## .vil File Format
.vil is from Vial - it doesn't contain enough information to properly render, so it currently imports from defaults. You can export your keymap from VIAL as a .vil file and reimport it later — useful for backing up your layout or sharing it with someone else who has the same keyboard.

## Svalboard Configuration
Remap keys, layers, macros, combos, and use tap-dance functions -- all without reflashing thanks to the magic of Vial. Default QWERTY, Colemak and Dvorak layouts are available, with many other community-generated options also available.

## Working with Layout Files
Use the configurator to save your current Vial keymap to .vil file before flashing (File → Save current layout). Then after flashing, load the saved keymap to restore it. This spares you the chore of recreating your keymap.

For Svalboard specifically, you can find pre-made configuration files in the svalboard-configs repository, which contains various layout options ending in .vil.

I found information about the Hands Down Neu layout by Alan Reiser. Here are the key findings:

## Home Block Design

The Hands Down Home Block consists of a 3x3 block of keys on each hand under index, middle, ring fingers, plus the resting positions of pinkies and thumbs, totaling 22 keys. These 22 keys define the prime real estate for keyboard design.

## Key Positions and Features

The layout demonstrates obsessive attention to finger movement in the "Home Block" to reduce fatigue during long typing sessions. There is a careful balance of usage frequency versus same-finger bigrams (SFBs) and distance/neighbors, delivering an exceptionally even typing rhythm.

Same-Finger Bigrams (SFBs) are exceptionally low, ensuring fingers are not abused hitting too many letters in a row with the same finger—identified as the single most important component of a good layout.

Hands Down Neu was released in 2021-08-04, and some Hands Down variations including Neu will work on keyboards with modifiers in standard ANSI/ISO/JIS slab keyboard positions on the pinkies, though the designer recommends split keyboards and home row modifiers.

# Hands Down Neu Layout

Based on the content provided, here is the exact Hands Down Neu key layout in a 3-row grid format:

**Top Row (Left to Right):**
w  f  m  p  v   /  .  q  "  '  z

**Home Row (Left to Right):**
r  s  n  t  b   ,  a  e  i  h  j

**Bottom Row (Left to Right):**
x  c  l  d  g   -  u  o  y  k

The layout organizes keys to minimize same-finger bigrams (SFBs) and maximize comfortable inward rolling motions. As described in the documentation, "Hands Down Neu variations are high alternation and high rolling with a strong preference for high in:out rolling ratio (approaching 3:1), very low SFBs overall."

The layout achieves 0.949% SFBs and works on standard ANSI keyboards without requiring special hardware modifications.

# Hands Down™ Neu Layout Grid

Based on the ANSI variant displayed on the page, here's the exact grid structure:

## Finger Block (3x5 per hand)
**Left Hand:**
- Row 1: Z J z | Q G q
- Row 2: A E C | I (thumb keys)
- Row 3: U O W | Y K

**Right Hand:**
- Row 1: M P V | R S N
- Row 2: (thumb keys) | H + - (thumb keys)
- Row 3: T B | X F L D

## Thumb Keys
The layout designates specific positions for thumb operation. The middle columns feature dedicated thumb-accessible keys, with "+ -" appearing in the thumb region between the two hand blocks.

**Note:** The interface shows multiple variant tabs (Dash, Élan, Gold, Silver, Bronze, Platinum, Titanium, Vibranium v/p/f/b, and Rhodium), each with slightly different character placements while maintaining this core 3x5+thumbs structure. The ANSI tab displays the primary version with punctuation and number-row symbols distributed across the grid's upper positions.

aiTitle: Configure svalboard with hands down neu

content.text:
Groundwork done. Facts first, then two decisions I need from you.

**What I found:**
1. Svalboard Lightly is plugged in (`303a:4044`, 5 input devices). No Svalboard/QMK/Vial config anywhere in `~/devel` — this is greenfield.
2. `svalboard/svalboard-configs` ships only QWERTY, Colemak-DHm, and blank `.vil`s. **No Hands Down.** So it has to be built.
3. I decoded the Svalboard `.vil` matrix from `SvalCOLEMAKDHM.vil` — 10 rows × 6 cols: row 0 = left thumb, rows 1–4 = L index/middle/ring/pinky, row 5 = right thumb, rows 6–9 = R index/middle/ring/pinky. Within a row: `[South, East, Center, North, West, unused]`. Verified against every Colemak-DHm letter.
4. Hyprland already does the right thing — the Svalboard isn't in your `device` list, so it falls through to the default plain `us` (your colemak variant is scoped to the two internal keyboards only). **No double-translation, no dotfiles change needed.**

**One correction to carry:** your stored HD Neu grid has `;` where alanreiser.com has `-`, and a duplicated `k`. Authoritative grid:

```
w f m p v   / . q " ' z
r s n t b   , a e i h j
x c l d g   - u o y k
```

Drovr gate: ran it — no methodology skill fits a greenfield keymap yet; I'll invoke `drovr:code-review` on the generated `.vil` before calling it done.

options.label: Generated .vil, checked into dotfiles (Recommended)
options.description: I write a script that takes SvalCOLEMAKDHM.vil as the base and rewrites the alpha positions to HD Neu, emitting a HandsDownNeu.vil. You load it in Vial/KeyBard. Repeatable and diffable; lives in the repo.

  SvalHandsDownNeu.vil

wrote SvalHandsDownNeu.vil (16 layers)
# then: KeyBard -> Load -> SvalHandsDownNeu.vil

options.label: Hand-authored .vil, no script
options.description: I write the .vil JSON directly, once. Simpler, but re-deriving it later means redoing the work by hand.

options.label: Step-by-step, you click it in
options.description: I give you a per-cup table (finger + direction -> key) and you enter it in KeyBard/Vial yourself. Nothing lands in the repo.

questions.question: What should the two thumb clusters do?

options.label: Keep Svalboard stock thumbs (Recommended)
options.description: Left: Ctrl Tab Shift Bksp Esc Gui. Right: Alt Enter MO(1) Space MO(2) Gui. Unchanged from the Colemak-DHm base — one variable at a time while you learn the alphas.
options.preview:
L thumb: LCTRL TAB LSHIFT BSPC ESC LGUI
R thumb: LALT ENTER MO(1) SPACE MO(2) LGUI

options.label: Hands Down-style thumbs
options.description: Rearrange toward Alan Reiser's recommendation: Space/Shift/Backspace/Enter on thumbs, layer keys on the outer thumb positions. Diverges from the base; more to relearn at once.

options.label: Add home-row mods too
options.description: Stock thumbs plus GACS home-row mods on the center (Down) keys of both hands. Biggest change; also the most likely to need tuning of tapping-term.

# "Glorious Engrammer" keymaps for MoErgo Glove80

These are [my Glove80][1] keymaps featuring the [Engram][2]([mer][3]) 
layouts with [Miryoku][4] layers and [home row mods][5].

[1]: https://sunaku.github.io/moergo-glove80-keyboard.html
[2]: https://sunaku.github.io/engram-keyboard-layout.html
[3]: https://sunaku.github.io/engrammer-keyboard-layout.html
[4]: https://github.com/manna-harbour/miryoku
[5]: https://sunaku.github.io/home-row-mods.html

## Legend

See [interactive layer map][6] for overview and documentation.  

NOTE: This is also available as a [printable PDF document][7].

[6]: https://sunaku.github.io/moergo-glove80-keyboard.html#layers
[7]: https://sunaku.github.io/moergo-glove80-keyboard-layers.pdf

Blocked on one thing, and it's a cheap unblock. Everything else is decoded and ready.

**Blocker: I can't read your Glove80 layout.**
- `sauyon/glove80-keymaps` is an unmodified fork of sunaku's (engram/engrammer, last push 2023) — not yours.
- `sauyon/zmk-config` has only `clog` and `two_percent_milk` keymaps — not Glove80.
- Nothing on disk, no export in `~/Downloads` (dir doesn't exist).
- Your layout lives in MoErgo's cloud. I probed their API: `my.glove80.com/api/layouts/v1/<uuid>` redirects to S3 and returned a well-formed `NoSuchKey` for the stale README UUID — meaning **a valid UUID probably does fetch without auth.**

**Do this (~30 seconds), pick either:**
1. Paste your `https://my.glove80.com/#/layout/user/<uuid>` URL. I'll pull the JSON myself.
2. Or: Advanced Settings → Enable local config → back to Edit → Download, then drop the `.json` anywhere and tell me the path.

**Why this blocks more than the symbols layer:** it also settles the alpha grid. The published HD Neu grid is ambiguous about which side the 6th column sits on — whether `h`/`j` land on right pinky or right index-inner. That's a materially different keymap and I won't guess it when your own working layout has the answer.

**Already done — the hard part.** I decoded the Svalboard matrix and the inner-column convention from `SvalCOLEMAKDHM.vil`:

```
rows: 0=L thumb, 1-4=L index/middle/ring/pinky
      5=R thumb, 6-9=R index/middle/ring/pinky
cols: [South, East, Center, North, West, unused]

inner column spills onto the East (left hand) / West (right hand) laterals:
  inner-top -> middle    inner-home -> index    inner-bottom -> ring
```

That rule reproduces Colemak-DHm exactly, so the generator is a straight table substitution once I have your grid.

**Assumption I'm carrying** (you skipped the thumbs question): stock Svalboard thumbs — `LCTRL TAB LSHIFT BSPC ESC LGUI` / `LALT ENTER MO(1) SPACE MO(2) LGUI`. Your Arensito symbols layer will land on `MO(1)`. Say so if the Glove80 puts symbols somewhere else.

Next action: paste the Glove80 URL.

Sources: [Hands Down Neu](https://sites.google.com/alanreiser.com/handsdown/home/hands-down-neu), [svalboard-configs](https://github.com/svalboard/svalboard-configs), [KeyBard](https://github.com/captdeaf/keybard)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Generate a Svalboard Vial keymap (.vil) for Hands Down Neu + Arensito symbols.

Source of truth for both layers is my Glove80 layout, exported from
my.glove80.com as glove80-hdneu.json (see README.md). This script re-expresses
that layout on the Svalboard's finger-cup geometry.

The base .vil is Svalboard's own SvalCOLEMAKDHM.vil, which supplies the thumb
clusters, the nav/F-key layer, and all the Vial metadata we don't want to
hand-author. We overwrite only the 40 finger-cup positions on layers 0 and 1.

Run `python3 build.py` to regenerate SvalHandsDownNeu.vil. The build refuses to
emit anything unless the self-test passes -- see check_mapping().
"""

import json
import pathlib
import sys

HERE = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent
BASE = HERE / "SvalCOLEMAKDHM.vil"
OUT = HERE / "SvalHandsDownNeu.vil"

# --- Svalboard .vil geometry -------------------------------------------------
#
# layout[layer] is 10 rows x 6 columns.
#
#   row 0 = left thumb cluster      row 5 = right thumb cluster
#   rows 1-4 = left  index, middle, ring, pinky
#   rows 6-9 = right index, middle, ring, pinky
#
# Within a finger row the columns are the five switches of that finger's cup,
# in absolute directions (East is always screen-right, on both hands):
#
#   [South, East, Center, North, unused]
#          col 0   col 1   col 2   col 3   col 4   col 5
#          South   East    Center  North   West    (unused, always -1)

S, E, C, N, W = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4

L_INDEX, L_MIDDLE, L_RING, L_PINKY = 1, 2, 3, 4
R_INDEX, R_MIDDLE, R_RING, R_PINKY = 6, 7, 8, 9

# A layout's alpha block is 3 rows x 5 columns. Column order runs outward-in on
# the left hand and inward-out on the right, matching how layouts are written:
#
#   left:  pinky ring middle index inner      right: inner index middle ring pinky
#
# The Svalboard has no dedicated inner-index column -- only four fingers. The
# stock Colemak-DHm config resolves this by spilling the inner column onto the
# inward-facing lateral of three different fingers:
#
#   inner-top -> middle    inner-home -> index    inner-bottom -> ring
#
# That inward lateral is East on the left hand and West on the right. We keep
# this convention so muscle memory transfers from Svalboard's own configs.

INNER_LATERAL = {"top": "middle", "home": "index", "bottom": "ring"}


def place(block, hand):
    """Map a 3x5 alpha block onto (row, col) -> keycode for one hand.

    block is {"top": [...5], "home": [...5], "bottom": [...5]} in the column
    order described above. Returns a dict suitable for splatting into a layer.
    """
    top, home, bottom = block["top"], block["home"], block["bottom"]

    if hand == "left":
        rows = {"pinky": L_PINKY, "ring": L_RING, "middle": L_MIDDLE, "index": L_INDEX}
        # left block columns, left to right
        cols = ["pinky", "ring", "middle", "index"]
        inner_col = 4
        lateral = E
    else:
        rows = {"pinky": R_PINKY, "ring": R_RING, "middle": R_MIDDLE, "index": R_INDEX}
        # right block columns run inner-first, so the finger columns are 1..4
        cols = ["index", "middle", "ring", "pinky"]
        inner_col = 0
        lateral = W

    out = {}
    for i, finger in enumerate(cols):
        col = i if hand == "left" else i + 1
        row = rows[finger]
        out[(row, N)] = top[col]
        out[(row, C)] = home[col]
        out[(row, S)] = bottom[col]

    for band, finger in INNER_LATERAL.items():
        out[(rows[finger], lateral)] = block[band][inner_col]

    return out


# --- Layer 0: Hands Down Neu -------------------------------------------------
#
#   w f m p v   / . q " ' z
#   r s n t b   , a e i h j
#   x c l d g   ; u o y k
#
# Exactly as it sits on the Glove80 today, including `;` on the right inner
# column (upstream Hands Down Neu publishes `-` there) and z/j on the outer
# column. The Svalboard has no outer column, so z and j go on the spare pinky
# laterals.

HDNEU_LEFT = {
    "top":    ["KC_W", "KC_F", "KC_M", "KC_P", "KC_V"],
    "home":   ["KC_R", "KC_S", "KC_N", "KC_T", "KC_B"],
    "bottom": ["KC_X", "KC_C", "KC_L", "KC_D", "KC_G"],
}

HDNEU_RIGHT = {
    "top":    ["KC_SLASH", "KC_DOT", "KC_Q", "LSFT(KC_QUOTE)", "KC_QUOTE"],
    "home":   ["KC_COMMA", "KC_A", "KC_E", "KC_I", "KC_H"],
    "bottom": ["KC_SCOLON", "KC_U", "KC_O", "KC_Y", "KC_K"],
}

# Glove80 outer column, rehomed onto spare Svalboard laterals. TAB/ESC/LSHIFT
# already live on the Svalboard's left thumb cluster, so only z and j need seats.
HDNEU_EXTRA = {
    (R_PINKY, E): "KC_Z",
    (R_PINKY, W): "KC_J",
}

# --- Layer 1: Arensito symbols ----------------------------------------------
#
#   { } [ ] @   & _ < > $
#   ; / - 0 :   \ 1 ( ) =
#   6 7 8 9 +   * 2 3 4 5
#
# Ported verbatim from the Glove80 "symbols" layer (reached there via &sl 3;
# here it is the MO(1) hold on the right thumb).

ARENSITO_LEFT = {
    "top":    ["LSFT(KC_LBRACKET)", "LSFT(KC_RBRACKET)", "KC_LBRACKET", "KC_RBRACKET", "LSFT(KC_2)"],
    "home":   ["KC_SCOLON", "KC_SLASH", "KC_MINUS", "KC_0", "LSFT(KC_SCOLON)"],
    "bottom": ["KC_6", "KC_7", "KC_8", "KC_9", "LSFT(KC_EQUAL)"],
}

ARENSITO_RIGHT = {
    "top":    ["LSFT(KC_7)", "LSFT(KC_MINUS)", "LSFT(KC_COMMA)", "LSFT(KC_DOT)", "LSFT(KC_4)"],
    "home":   ["KC_BSLASH", "KC_1", "LSFT(KC_9)", "LSFT(KC_0)", "KC_EQUAL"],
    "bottom": ["LSFT(KC_8)", "KC_2", "KC_3", "KC_4", "KC_5"],
}

# Spare laterals on the symbol layer fall through to the base layer rather than
# keeping Colemak's leftovers.
FINGER_ROWS = [L_INDEX, L_MIDDLE, L_RING, L_PINKY, R_INDEX, R_MIDDLE, R_RING, R_PINKY]


# --- Self-test ---------------------------------------------------------------
#
# place() encodes a guess about Svalboard's matrix order that, if wrong, would
# produce a plausible-looking but scrambled keymap. So we run the stock
# Colemak-DHm block back through place() and require it to reproduce the
# shipped SvalCOLEMAKDHM.vil alpha positions exactly.

COLEMAK_LEFT = {
    "top":    ["KC_Q", "KC_W", "KC_F", "KC_P", "KC_B"],
    "home":   ["KC_A", "KC_R", "KC_S", "KC_T", "KC_G"],
    "bottom": ["KC_Z", "KC_X", "KC_C", "KC_D", "KC_V"],
}

COLEMAK_RIGHT = {
    "top":    ["KC_J", "KC_L", "KC_U", "KC_Y", "KC_SCOLON"],
    "home":   ["KC_M", "KC_N", "KC_E", "KC_I", "KC_O"],
    "bottom": ["KC_K", "KC_H", "KC_COMMA", "KC_DOT", "KC_SLASH"],
}


def check_mapping(base_layer0):
    """Reproduce Colemak-DHm through place(); compare against the shipped .vil."""
    rebuilt = {}
    rebuilt.update(place(COLEMAK_LEFT, "left"))
    rebuilt.update(place(COLEMAK_RIGHT, "right"))

    bad = []
    for (row, col), want in sorted(rebuilt.items()):
        got = base_layer0[row][col]
        if got != want:
            bad.append(f"  r{row}c{col}: base has {got}, mapping produced {want}")

    if bad:
        raise SystemExit(
            "self-test FAILED -- place() does not reproduce Colemak-DHm:\n"
            + "\n".join(bad)
        )
    return len(rebuilt)


def main():
    if not BASE.exists():
        raise SystemExit(
            f"missing {BASE.name}. Fetch it with:\n"
            "  gh api repos/svalboard/svalboard-configs/contents/SvalCOLEMAKDHM.vil "
            f"--jq .content | base64 -d > {BASE}"
        )

    vil = json.loads(BASE.read_text())
    layers = vil["layout"]

    checked = check_mapping(layers[0])
    print(f"self-test OK: {checked} Colemak-DHm positions reproduced from place()")

    base = {}
    base.update(place(HDNEU_LEFT, "left"))
    base.update(place(HDNEU_RIGHT, "right"))
    base.update(HDNEU_EXTRA)
    for (row, col), code in base.items():
        layers[0][row][col] = code

    # Blank the finger cups on layer 1 so Colemak's symbol layer can't show
    # through on positions Arensito doesn't use.
    for row in FINGER_ROWS:
        for col in (S, E, C, N, W):
            layers[1][row][col] = "KC_TRNS"

    sym = {}
    sym.update(place(ARENSITO_LEFT, "left"))
    sym.update(place(ARENSITO_RIGHT, "right"))
    for (row, col), code in sym.items():
        layers[1][row][col] = code

    OUT.write_text(json.dumps(vil, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(f"wrote {OUT.name}: {len(base)} base + {len(sym)} symbol positions, "
          f"{len(layers)} layers")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

COLEMAK_RIGHT = {
    "top":    ["KC_J", "KC_L", "KC_U", "KC_Y", "KC_SCOLON"],
    "home":   ["KC_M", "KC_N", "KC_E", "KC_I", "KC_O"],
    "bottom": ["KC_K", "KC_H", "KC_COMMA", "KC_DOT", "KC_SLASH"],
}


def check_mapping(base_layer0):
    """Reproduce Colemak-DHm through place(); compare against the shipped .vil."""
    rebuilt = {}
    rebuilt.update(place(COLEMAK_LEFT, "left"))
    rebuilt.update(place(COLEMAK_RIGHT, "right"))

    bad = []
    for (row, col), want in sorted(rebuilt.items()):
        got = base_layer0[row][col]
        if got != want:
            bad.append(f"  r{row}c{col}: base has {got}, mapping produced {want}")

    if bad:
        raise SystemExit(
            "self-test FAILED -- place() does not reproduce Colemak-DHm:\n"
            + "\n".join(bad)
        )
    return len(rebuilt)


def main():
    if not BASE.exists():
        raise SystemExit(
            f"missing {BASE.name}. Fetch it with:\n"
            "  gh api repos/svalboard/svalboard-configs/contents/SvalCOLEMAKDHM.vil "
            f"--jq .content | base64 -d > {BASE}"
        )

    vil = json.loads(BASE.read_text())
    layers = vil["layout"]

    checked = check_mapping(layers[0])
    print(f"self-test OK: {checked} Colemak-DHm positions reproduced from place()")

    base = {}
    base.update(place(HDNEU_LEFT, "left"))
    base.update(place(HDNEU_RIGHT, "right"))
    base.update(HDNEU_EXTRA)
    for (row, col), code in base.items():
        layers[0][row][col] = code

    # Blank the finger cups on layer 1 so Colemak's symbol layer can't show
    # through on positions Arensito doesn't use.
    for row in FINGER_ROWS:
        for col in (S, E, C, N, W):
            layers[1][row][col] = "KC_TRNS"

    sym = {}
    sym.update(place(ARENSITO_LEFT, "left"))
    sym.update(place(ARENSITO_RIGHT, "right"))
    for (row, col), code in sym.items():
        layers[1][row][col] = code

    OUT.write_text(json.dumps(vil, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(f"wrote {OUT.name}: {len(base)} base + {len(sym)} symbol positions, "
          f"{len(layers)} layers")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

input.content:
# Svalboard — Hands Down Neu + Arensito symbols

Vial keymap for the Svalboard Lightly, ported from my Glove80.

## Load it

1. Open [KeyBard](https://captdeaf.github.io/keybard/) (or the Vial app) with the
   Svalboard plugged in.
2. **Load** → `SvalHandsDownNeu.vil`.

No reflash needed — Vial writes the keymap to the keyboard live.

## Layers

**Layer 0 — Hands Down Neu**

```
w f m p v   / . q " '
r s n t b   , a e i h
x c l d g   ; u o y k
```

`z` and `j` sit on the right pinky's East and West laterals. On the Glove80 they
live in the outer column, which the Svalboard doesn't have.

Note this is my Glove80's Neu, not upstream's: `;` on the right inner column
where [alanreiser.com](https://sites.google.com/alanreiser.com/handsdown/home/hands-down-neu)
publishes `-`.

**Layer 1 — Arensito symbols** (hold `MO(1)`, right thumb)

```
{ } [ ] @   & _ < > $
; / - 0 :   \ 1 ( ) =
6 7 8 9 +   * 2 3 4 5
```

**Layer 2** — nav and F-keys, untouched from Svalboard's stock config.

Thumb clusters are also stock:

```
L: ctrl tab shift bspc esc gui
R: alt enter MO(1) space MO(2) gui
```

## Host setup

Nothing to do. Hyprland scopes my Colemak variant to the two internal keyboards
by device name (`hyprland.nix`), so the Svalboard falls through to the default
plain `us` — which is what a firmware-side layout wants. Adding the Svalboard to
that `device` list would double-translate every keystroke.

## Regenerating

```sh
python3 build.py
```

`build.py` rewrites the 40 finger-cup positions on layers 0 and 1 of
`SvalCOLEMAKDHM.vil` (vendored from
[svalboard/svalboard-configs](https://github.com/svalboard/svalboard-configs)),
leaving thumbs, layer 2, and Vial metadata alone.

The interesting part is the geometry. Svalboard `.vil` layers are 10×6:

```
row 0 = left thumb        row 5 = right thumb
rows 1-4 = left  index, middle, ring, pinky
rows 6-9 = right index, middle, ring, pinky
cols     = [South, East, Center, North, West, unused]
```

Each finger has only N/C/S for its column, so the layout's inner-index column
spills onto one inward lateral per finger — `inner-top → middle`,
`inner-home → index`, `inner-bottom → ring`. That convention is Svalboard's own,
reverse-engineered from their Colemak-DHm config.

Since that mapping is a guess about matrix order that would fail *silently* —
producing a scrambled but valid-looking keymap — `build.py` refuses to emit
anything until it has run the stock Colemak-DHm block back through the same code
path and reproduced all 30 alpha positions in the shipped `.vil` exactly.

## Source

Glove80 layout `e3409150-bb22-49c0-8614-10035f3f6a04` ("Sauyon layout
2026-01-20"), layer `Base` and layer `symbols`.

Base directory for this skill: /nix/store/6fy9flk1ym9bgpgx9df6payz4yplrx14-source/skills/code-review

# Code Review

## Overview

**They find, you fix.** Follow the spirit, not the letter: dispatching a
reviewer satisfies the letter; one that read an empty diff, or that you never
waited for, looked at nothing and found nothing. The rule is that
somebody who did not write the change has said what is wrong with it — and that
cannot be you. You read the change you meant to make, not the one on disk.

**Write for the agent who inherits this: the next phase agent is you, with your
context gone.** A finding you settled in your head is one they meet as a bug,
with nothing saying anyone saw it.

## The Iron Law

```
NO CHANGE IS DONE UNTIL A READ-ONLY REVIEWER HAS SEEN IT AND
EVERY CRITICAL AND IMPORTANT FINDING IS RESOLVED OR RECORDED AS DEFERRED.
```

**Read-only** is a trust boundary, not a performance note: the reviewer reads
anything, runs read-only checks, and writes nothing — not source, not git, not
run state. You stay the single writer.

No exceptions:

- **Never run a reviewer in the background.** Do not set `run_in_background`,
  do not yield, and do not schedule a wakeup while one is out. A backgrounded
  reviewer parks you mid-turn, indistinguishable from a finished turn, and the
  run stalls until a human nudges the pane. Dispatch it blocking and read its
  verdict in the turn you dispatched it.
- **Do not judge a change too small to review.** A one-line edit to a condition
  is the size this skill exists for. Dispatch a reviewer over it.
- **Do not count your own read as the review.** Re-reading your diff tells you
  it matches what you intended — the one thing never in doubt. Dispatch someone
  who does not know it.
- **Do not leave it for the pipeline's review phase.** That phase reads what you
  hand it, after later work is built on it. Dispatch here, while the change is
  one commit wide.
- **Do not close a finding by disagreeing with it.** When you will not fix one,
  quote it and write the reason in the report or handoff. An unrecorded
  decision reads downstream like an unread finding.
- **Do not repeat a verdict you have not read.** Open the file the reviewer
  names, or re-run the review when it named none. A reviewer that never came
  back has not said "clean".

## Announce

Say this out loud before dispatching anything:

```
Using drovr:code-review — dispatching read-only reviewers before calling this done.
```

## The procedure

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

Re-create those items for each change you review, not once for the session.

1. **Write down the change and the exact range** — the files, and `<base>..HEAD`.
   Get it wrong and the reviewer reports clean on nothing.
2. **Dispatch read-only reviewers, blocking, one per angle:** run
   `drovr code-review run <run> <task>` (`<base>` from `<task>-base.sha`, recorded
   before your first edit) — or, **inline** with no run,
   `drovr code-review run --base "$(git merge-base HEAD main)" <task>`. Nothing
   else, and never invent a run to get one.

   It spawns one reviewer per **configured** angle — `config.angles`, which
   defaults to correctness, security, error-handling, type-design — each writing
   `<task>-review-<angle>.json`, merged into `<task>-review.json`. **Read the
   config, not this page**, and cover any lens it omits yourself.

   Tell each reviewer to review as a skeptic, not the author; to say whether the
   tests exercise the behaviour, not just that they pass; to rate every finding
   **Critical, Important or nit** — what the Iron Law gates on — and say so when
   it found none; and to write them to a path you name, so step 3 has something
   to open. The lenses to cover:
   - **Spec compliance** — what was agreed, no more, no less?
   - **Correctness** — real bugs, unhandled cases, broken invariants.
   - **Verification** — do the claimed tests exist, and would they fail on a
     regression?
   - **Quality** — reuse, simplification, consistency with the code around it.
3. **Wait for every reviewer, then read what each wrote.** Open the findings
   file by path. Exit codes: 0 clean, 3 findings, 2 timeout, 1 error — **only 0
   is clean**, and a reviewer that returned no verdict is none of the four.
   Re-dispatch rather than report its silence.
4. **Check what the reviewer actually read — range *and* working tree.** The
   range must be the whole of `<base>..HEAD`, every file you touched, not a
   subset you picked; **and uncommitted work is in scope, not exempt** — drovr's
   panel reviews the diff *plus the current working tree*. A verdict covers what
   is on disk only if the reviewer saw both. Clean on an empty range, a subset,
   or a tree with unreviewed edits in it is about a change nobody read.
5. **Resolve every Critical and Important finding, or record the deferral.**
   Per finding: quote it, then name the edit answering it by file or write down
   why you are not making it.
6. **Re-run the checks after your last review-driven edit, then say it is
   done.** The fixes are new, unverified code: run the tests. When the change is
   not code and has no suite, name what you re-read instead and why it covers the
   edits — written down, never assumed. Report the findings, the edits and the
   deferrals; inside a drovr phase this also gates `drovr phase done`.

## Requirements

The middle column is what the claim takes; the right is what gets accepted
instead.

| The claim | Required evidence | NOT sufficient |
|---|---|---|
| *"This change has been reviewed"* | A read-only reviewer dispatched over this change in the foreground, returned in this turn, and the range you handed it, written down | Your own re-read · a reviewer launched and not waited for · a review of the tree before your last edit |
| *"The reviewer found nothing"* | The findings file it wrote, opened by path and read by you — or the review re-run by you when it wrote none — **and** what it read shown to be the whole of `<base>..HEAD` **plus your working tree** | Its summary, however much output it pastes · exit 1 or 2 · a subset of your files · uncommitted edits nobody looked at · a verdict that never arrived |
| *"Every Critical and Important finding is resolved"* | Each quoted, the edit answering it named by file, and step 6's checks re-run after the last edit | A count · agreeing with one in prose · fixing the Criticals and leaving the Importants |
| *"That finding does not apply here"* | The finding quoted, and the reason written where the next agent reads it | Deciding it in your head · *"out of scope"* with no scope named · silence, which downstream reads as resolved |

## Red flags — STOP

Some are thoughts, some are things you have just written. Either way you are at
the line.

- *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* · *"The lead said just
  send it."* · *"It is a two-line change."* · *"I already reviewed it myself."*
  · *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* — each opens a row in
  *Rationalizations*, verbatim. Go do the thing in its row.
- *You are about to launch a reviewer in the background and keep working.* →
  Dispatch it blocking. No version of that ends with you reading its verdict
  this turn.
- *A reviewer has not come back and you are writing the report.* → Block on it.
  Silence is not a pass; a parked reviewer is not a finished one.
- *The panel came back clean in seconds on a large diff.* → Check what it read.
  Clean and empty look identical from here.
- **Anything that treats the change as finished** — any wording at all, and
  also committing, opening a PR, or starting the next task — while a reviewer is
  unread, unreturned, or holding an unresolved Critical or Important finding. If
  you cannot name the reviewer and point at what it wrote, change what you
  dispatched, not how you word it.

## Rationalizations

The right column is an instruction, not an argument. Do the thing in it.

| The thought | Do this instead |
|---|---|
| *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* | Dispatch the reviewer first, then send it. Two different reads: theirs is for fit, the review's is for correctness, and one does not make the other redundant — reading a document aloud catches prose gaps, not retry semantics. |
| *"The lead said just send it."* | Send it after the review, and tell them the call moves. That is a scheduling reflex, not anyone weighing the technical risk — the calendar is theirs, the correctness yours. |
| *"It is a two-line change."* | Dispatch a reviewer over the two lines. Size is not a risk measure, and the risk you estimate in order to skip the review is what it would have told you. |
| *"I already reviewed it myself."* | Dispatch one that did not write it. Your read confirms the diff matches your intent; the defects worth catching are in what you did not think of. |
| *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* | Dispatch here, now. That phase reads what you hand it, after later tasks built on it; a finding costs more at every step it survives. |
| *"The reviewer came back with no findings."* | Open the file it named, and check it read your whole change, working tree included. An empty range comes back clean from every angle at once. |

## Worked example

Condensed from a real decision: a 320-line spec, a client call in 19 minutes
where three people read it aloud, a $45,000 sign-off, the lead writing
*"just send it."* Reviewer output is illustrative, not a transcript.

❌ **What this looks like when it fails:**

> They are going to read it out loud section by section — that *is* the review,
> and a review pass first is a second reading of something nobody has read
> once. The lead said send it. Sending.

✅ **What it looks like when it holds:**

> Using drovr:code-review — dispatching read-only reviewers before calling this
> done. The "second reading" framing conflates two reads: theirs is for fit,
> the review's is for correctness, and one does not make the other redundant.
> "Just send it" is a scheduling call; the retry semantics are mine. Moving the
> call:

```
$ drovr code-review run warehouse-sync spec
reviewed 320 lines (a41c9e2..HEAD) · 4/4 angles returned
correctness    IMPORTANT §4.2 retry window (30s) < the 45s ack timeout in §3.1
error-handling IMPORTANT §6 reconciliation excludes the partial-day boundary
type-design    nit       §2 names two ids for one endpoint
exit 3
```

> Both Importants fixed in `spec/warehouse-sync.md` — retry window 30s → 60s, §6
> reconciliation now spans the boundary day — from `spec-review.json`, not the
> summary line. A spec has no suite, so step 6 here is both edited
> sections re-read against §3.1, not assumed. The nit is deferred
> and recorded here: the duplicate id is in a section the client wrote, and
> renaming it would confuse the walkthrough. Sent 22 minutes late, call moved:
> that window would have shipped a contract we could not meet.

## Cross-refs

- `drovr:verification-before-completion` — REQUIRED before you repeat a
  verdict: a reviewer's report is a claim, not evidence.
- `drovr:systematic-debugging` — REQUIRED when a finding is a bug: it is a
  report, not a diagnosis. Reproduce before you fix.
- `drovr:tdd` — REQUIRED when a finding needs new behaviour: the fix is new code
  and gets a failing test.
- `drovr:handoff` — REQUIRED at a phase boundary: deferred findings travel in the
  handoff or not at all.


ARGUMENTS: --base HEAD

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Generate a Svalboard Vial keymap (.vil) for Hands Down Neu + Arensito symbols.

Source of truth for both layers is my Glove80 layout, exported from
my.glove80.com as glove80-hdneu.json (see README.md). This script re-expresses
that layout on the Svalboard's finger-cup geometry.

The base .vil is Svalboard's own SvalCOLEMAKDHM.vil, which supplies the thumb
clusters, the nav/F-key layer, and all the Vial metadata we don't want to
hand-author. We overwrite only the 40 finger-cup positions on layers 0 and 1.

Run `python3 build.py` to regenerate SvalHandsDownNeu.vil. The build refuses to
emit anything unless the self-test passes -- see check_mapping().
"""

import json
import pathlib
import sys

HERE = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent
BASE = HERE / "SvalCOLEMAKDHM.vil"
OUT = HERE / "SvalHandsDownNeu.vil"

# --- Svalboard .vil geometry -------------------------------------------------
#
# layout[layer] is 10 rows x 6 columns.
#
#   row 0 = left thumb cluster      row 5 = right thumb cluster
#   rows 1-4 = left  index, middle, ring, pinky
#   rows 6-9 = right index, middle, ring, pinky
#
# Within a finger row the columns are the five switches of that finger's cup,
# in absolute directions (East is always screen-right, on both hands):
#
#   [South, East, Center, North, unused]
#          col 0   col 1   col 2   col 3   col 4   col 5
#          South   East    Center  North   West    (unused, always -1)

S, E, C, N, W = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4

L_INDEX, L_MIDDLE, L_RING, L_PINKY = 1, 2, 3, 4
R_INDEX, R_MIDDLE, R_RING, R_PINKY = 6, 7, 8, 9

# A layout's alpha block is 3 rows x 5 columns. Column order runs outward-in on
# the left hand and inward-out on the right, matching how layouts are written:
#
#   left:  pinky ring middle index inner      right: inner index middle ring pinky
#
# The Svalboard has no dedicated inner-index column -- only four fingers. The
# stock Colemak-DHm config resolves this by spilling the inner column onto the
# inward-facing lateral of three different fingers:
#
#   inner-top -> middle    inner-home -> index    inner-bottom -> ring
#
# That inward lateral is East on the left hand and West on the right. We keep
# this convention so muscle memory transfers from Svalboard's own configs.

INNER_LATERAL = {"top": "middle", "home": "index", "bottom": "ring"}


def place(block, hand):
    """Map a 3x5 alpha block onto (row, col) -> keycode for one hand.

    block is {"top": [...5], "home": [...5], "bottom": [...5]} in the column
    order described above. Returns a dict suitable for splatting into a layer.
    """
    top, home, bottom = block["top"], block["home"], block["bottom"]

    if hand == "left":
        rows = {"pinky": L_PINKY, "ring": L_RING, "middle": L_MIDDLE, "index": L_INDEX}
        # left block columns, left to right
        cols = ["pinky", "ring", "middle", "index"]
        inner_col = 4
        lateral = E
    else:
        rows = {"pinky": R_PINKY, "ring": R_RING, "middle": R_MIDDLE, "index": R_INDEX}
        # right block columns run inner-first, so the finger columns are 1..4
        cols = ["index", "middle", "ring", "pinky"]
        inner_col = 0
        lateral = W

    out = {}
    for i, finger in enumerate(cols):
        col = i if hand == "left" else i + 1
        row = rows[finger]
        out[(row, N)] = top[col]
        out[(row, C)] = home[col]
        out[(row, S)] = bottom[col]

    for band, finger in INNER_LATERAL.items():
        out[(rows[finger], lateral)] = block[band][inner_col]

    return out


# --- Layer 0: Hands Down Neu -------------------------------------------------
#
#   w f m p v   / . q " ' z
#   r s n t b   , a e i h j
#   x c l d g   ; u o y k
#
# Exactly as it sits on the Glove80 today, including `;` on the right inner
# column (upstream Hands Down Neu publishes `-` there) and z/j on the outer
# column. The Svalboard has no outer column, so z and j go on the spare pinky
# laterals.

HDNEU_LEFT = {
    "top":    ["KC_W", "KC_F", "KC_M", "KC_P", "KC_V"],
    "home":   ["KC_R", "KC_S", "KC_N", "KC_T", "KC_B"],
    "bottom": ["KC_X", "KC_C", "KC_L", "KC_D", "KC_G"],
}

HDNEU_RIGHT = {
    "top":    ["KC_SLASH", "KC_DOT", "KC_Q", "LSFT(KC_QUOTE)", "KC_QUOTE"],
    "home":   ["KC_COMMA", "KC_A", "KC_E", "KC_I", "KC_H"],
    "bottom": ["KC_SCOLON", "KC_U", "KC_O", "KC_Y", "KC_K"],
}

# Glove80 outer column, rehomed onto spare Svalboard laterals. TAB/ESC/LSHIFT
# already live on the Svalboard's left thumb cluster, so only z and j need seats.
HDNEU_EXTRA = {
    (R_PINKY, E): "KC_Z",
    (R_PINKY, W): "KC_J",
}

# --- Layer 1: Arensito symbols ----------------------------------------------
#
#   { } [ ] @   & _ < > $
#   ; / - 0 :   \ 1 ( ) =
#   6 7 8 9 +   * 2 3 4 5
#
# Ported verbatim from the Glove80 "symbols" layer (reached there via &sl 3;
# here it is the MO(1) hold on the right thumb).

ARENSITO_LEFT = {
    "top":    ["LSFT(KC_LBRACKET)", "LSFT(KC_RBRACKET)", "KC_LBRACKET", "KC_RBRACKET", "LSFT(KC_2)"],
    "home":   ["KC_SCOLON", "KC_SLASH", "KC_MINUS", "KC_0", "LSFT(KC_SCOLON)"],
    "bottom": ["KC_6", "KC_7", "KC_8", "KC_9", "LSFT(KC_EQUAL)"],
}

ARENSITO_RIGHT = {
    "top":    ["LSFT(KC_7)", "LSFT(KC_MINUS)", "LSFT(KC_COMMA)", "LSFT(KC_DOT)", "LSFT(KC_4)"],
    "home":   ["KC_BSLASH", "KC_1", "LSFT(KC_9)", "LSFT(KC_0)", "KC_EQUAL"],
    "bottom": ["LSFT(KC_8)", "KC_2", "KC_3", "KC_4", "KC_5"],
}

# Spare laterals on the symbol layer fall through to the base layer rather than
# keeping Colemak's leftovers.
FINGER_ROWS = [L_INDEX, L_MIDDLE, L_RING, L_PINKY, R_INDEX, R_MIDDLE, R_RING, R_PINKY]


# --- Self-test ---------------------------------------------------------------
#
# place() encodes a guess about Svalboard's matrix order that, if wrong, would
# produce a plausible-looking but scrambled keymap. So we run the stock
# Colemak-DHm block back through place() and require it to reproduce the
# shipped SvalCOLEMAKDHM.vil alpha positions exactly.

COLEMAK_LEFT = {
    "top":    ["KC_Q", "KC_W", "KC_F", "KC_P", "KC_B"],
    "home":   ["KC_A", "KC_R", "KC_S", "KC_T", "KC_G"],
    "bottom": ["KC_Z", "KC_X", "KC_C", "KC_D", "KC_V"],
}

COLEMAK_RIGHT = {
    "top":    ["KC_J", "KC_L", "KC_U", "KC_Y", "KC_SCOLON"],
    "home":   ["KC_M", "KC_N", "KC_E", "KC_I", "KC_O"],
    "bottom": ["KC_K", "KC_H", "KC_COMMA", "KC_DOT", "KC_SLASH"],
}


def check_mapping(base_layer0):
    """Reproduce Colemak-DHm through place(); compare against the shipped .vil."""
    rebuilt = {}
    rebuilt.update(place(COLEMAK_LEFT, "left"))
    rebuilt.update(place(COLEMAK_RIGHT, "right"))

    bad = []
    for (row, col), want in sorted(rebuilt.items()):
        got = base_layer0[row][col]
        if got != want:
            bad.append(f"  r{row}c{col}: base has {got}, mapping produced {want}")

    if bad:
        raise SystemExit(
            "self-test FAILED -- place() does not reproduce Colemak-DHm:\n"
            + "\n".join(bad)
        )
    return len(rebuilt)


def main():
    if not BASE.exists():
        raise SystemExit(
            f"missing {BASE.name}. Fetch it with:\n"
            "  gh api repos/svalboard/svalboard-configs/contents/SvalCOLEMAKDHM.vil "
            f"--jq .content | base64 -d > {BASE}"
        )

    vil = json.loads(BASE.read_text())
    layers = vil["layout"]

    checked = check_mapping(layers[0])
    print(f"self-test OK: {checked} Colemak-DHm positions reproduced from place()")

    base = {}
    base.update(place(HDNEU_LEFT, "left"))
    base.update(place(HDNEU_RIGHT, "right"))
    base.update(HDNEU_EXTRA)
    for (row, col), code in base.items():
        layers[0][row][col] = code

    # Blank the finger cups on layer 1 so Colemak's symbol layer can't show
    # through on positions Arensito doesn't use.
    for row in FINGER_ROWS:
        for col in (S, E, C, N, W):
            layers[1][row][col] = "KC_TRNS"

    sym = {}
    sym.update(place(ARENSITO_LEFT, "left"))
    sym.update(place(ARENSITO_RIGHT, "right"))
    for (row, col), code in sym.items():
        layers[1][row][col] = code

    OUT.write_text(json.dumps(vil, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(f"wrote {OUT.name}: {len(base)} base + {len(sym)} symbol positions, "
          f"{len(layers)} layers")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

# Svalboard — Hands Down Neu + Arensito symbols

Vial keymap for the Svalboard Lightly, ported from my Glove80.

## Load it

1. Open [KeyBard](https://captdeaf.github.io/keybard/) (or the Vial app) with the
   Svalboard plugged in.
2. **Load** → `SvalHandsDownNeu.vil`.

No reflash needed — Vial writes the keymap to the keyboard live.

## Layers

**Layer 0 — Hands Down Neu**

```
w f m p v   / . q " '
r s n t b   , a e i h
x c l d g   ; u o y k
```

`z` and `j` sit on the right pinky's East and West laterals. On the Glove80 they
live in the outer column, which the Svalboard doesn't have.

Note this is my Glove80's Neu, not upstream's: `;` on the right inner column
where [alanreiser.com](https://sites.google.com/alanreiser.com/handsdown/home/hands-down-neu)
publishes `-`.

**Layer 1 — Arensito symbols** (hold `MO(1)`, right thumb)

```
{ } [ ] @   & _ < > $
; / - 0 :   \ 1 ( ) =
6 7 8 9 +   * 2 3 4 5
```

**Layer 2** — nav and F-keys, untouched from Svalboard's stock config.

Thumb clusters are also stock:

```
L: ctrl tab shift bspc esc gui
R: alt enter MO(1) space MO(2) gui
```

## Host setup

Nothing to do. Hyprland scopes my Colemak variant to the two internal keyboards
by device name (`hyprland.nix`), so the Svalboard falls through to the default
plain `us` — which is what a firmware-side layout wants. Adding the Svalboard to
that `device` list would double-translate every keystroke.

## Regenerating

```sh
python3 build.py
```

`build.py` rewrites the 40 finger-cup positions on layers 0 and 1 of
`SvalCOLEMAKDHM.vil` (vendored from
[svalboard/svalboard-configs](https://github.com/svalboard/svalboard-configs)),
leaving thumbs, layer 2, and Vial metadata alone.

The interesting part is the geometry. Svalboard `.vil` layers are 10×6:

```
row 0 = left thumb        row 5 = right thumb
rows 1-4 = left  index, middle, ring, pinky
rows 6-9 = right index, middle, ring, pinky
cols     = [South, East, Center, North, West, unused]
```

Each finger has only N/C/S for its column, so the layout's inner-index column
spills onto one inward lateral per finger — `inner-top → middle`,
`inner-home → index`, `inner-bottom → ring`. That convention is Svalboard's own,
reverse-engineered from their Colemak-DHm config.

Since that mapping is a guess about matrix order that would fail *silently* —
producing a scrambled but valid-looking keymap — `build.py` refuses to emit
anything until it has run the stock Colemak-DHm block back through the same code
path and reproduced all 30 alpha positions in the shipped `.vil` exactly.

column-order comment that omitted West is gone.

directly into chat, or export it: Advanced Settings → Enable local config → back
to Edit → Download.

Root cause found — and it means installing Vial alone would *not* have fixed it.

So it's two things: a udev rule (needs root) **and** the app.

=== system/deploy ===
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Run as your normal user (e.g. `mise run deploy`), NOT under sudo: the sops
# steps below decrypt with your GCP key under $HOME and each privileged install
# sudo's itself. Running the whole script as root points $HOME at /root, so sops
# can't find the key (and root has no KMS creds) -- fail fast instead.
if [ "$(id -u)" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "system/deploy: run as your user (try 'mise run system:deploy'), not root." >&2
  exit 1
fi

cd "$(dirname "$0")"
find etc/ -type d | while read -r d; do sudo mkdir -p "/${d}"; done
find etc/ -type f | while read -r f; do sudo cp -v "${f}" "/${f}"; done

# polkit only scans /usr/share/polkit-1/actions for action definitions, which
# etc/ can't reach; install Bitwarden's unlock action there so its "system
# authentication" biometric prompt is authorized on this non-NixOS host.
sudo install -Dvm644 polkit-1/actions/com.bitwarden.Bitwarden.policy \
  /usr/share/polkit-1/actions/com.bitwarden.Bitwarden.policy

# ── gnome-keyring: let the home-manager unit own the daemon ───────────────────
# The login collection can only be unlocked at daemon startup, so home-manager
# runs its own gnome-keyring.service whose ExecStart unseals the passphrase from
# the TPM (see gnome-keyring-tpm in home.nix). Mask Arch's packaged units so a
# second, *locked* daemon can't be started behind our back -- its socket unit
# listens on %t/keyring/control and would socket-activate one on any control-op.
# This is only half the job: the D-Bus activation files in /usr/share also start
# a locked daemon, and systemd masking does nothing about those. They are
# shadowed from ~/.local/share/dbus-1/services by home.nix.
sudo rm -f /etc/systemd/user/sockets.target.wants/gnome-keyring-daemon.socket
sudo ln -sfn /dev/null /etc/systemd/user/gnome-keyring-daemon.socket
sudo ln -sfn /dev/null /etc/systemd/user/gnome-keyring-daemon.service

# Unsealing the gnome-keyring passphrase reads /dev/tpmrm0, which is root:tss 0660.
# Takes effect at next login, not in the current session.
if ! id -nG "$USER" | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -qx tss; then
  sudo gpasswd -a "$USER" tss
fi

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
# systemd-oomd parses oomd.conf (and its drop-ins) once at startup, so a changed
# etc/systemd/oomd.conf.d/* must be followed by an actual restart. `enable --now`
# is NOT enough: --now only *starts* a stopped unit, so on a host where oomd is
# already running it is a silent no-op and the new limits sit on disk unapplied.
# `restart` covers both cases (starts it if stopped) and kills nothing on its way
# through -- oomd holds no state worth preserving across a reload.
sudo systemctl enable systemd-oomd
sudo systemctl restart systemd-oomd

# ── drovr review server firewall ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# `drovr serve` binds 0.0.0.0 on this host and has NO authentication, so the
# allowlist in etc/nftables.d/drovr.nft is the only thing between the pod network
# and every run's contents. `restart` rather than `enable --now`, for the same
# reason as oomd above: --now is a no-op on an already-active unit, which would
# leave an edited ruleset sitting on disk unapplied.
#
# NOTE the unit loads its own `inet drovr` table and nothing else. Do NOT enable
# nftables.service to persist this instead: Arch ships /etc/nftables.conf as a

content.text: Making the changes. Rule matches the vial magic serial, so it covers every Vial board rather than hardcoding Svalboard's VID.

input.content:
# Vial-compatible keyboards (Svalboard Lightly and friends).
#
# The config interface is a /dev/hidraw* node, which udev creates 0600 root:root
# by default. Without this rule Vial and browser-based KeyBard both enumerate the
# keyboard and then fail to open it -- the failure surfaces as "no keyboard
# detected", with nothing pointing at permissions.
#
# Matching the vial magic serial rather than VID/PID covers every Vial board on
# one rule, which is what upstream's own rule does. Verified against this host:
#   /sys/bus/usb/devices/9-1.4.1.2/serial = vial:f64c2b3c
#
# TAG+="uaccess" is the mechanism that normally does the work -- logind puts an
# ACL on the node for whoever owns the active seat. GROUP is the fallback for
# sessions logind doesn't treat as seated, which is a live concern on this host
# (systemd-homed user, uid 60006, absent from /etc/passwd -- see home.nix). Note
# upstream's rule says GROUP="users", which would be a no-op here: sauyon is in
# input, video, audio, wheel, realtime, docker and tss, but not users.
KERNEL=="hidraw*", SUBSYSTEM=="hidraw", ATTRS{serial}=="*vial:f64c2b3c*", MODE="0660", GROUP="input", TAG+="uaccess", TAG+="udev-acl"

content.text:
Fixed and verified. One thing needs your call.

**It works now — try it: run `Vial`** (capitalized — that's the binary name).

**The actual problem was never the software.** Your Svalboard's `/dev/hidraw*` nodes were `0600 root:root`. Browser KeyBard enumerated the keyboard via WebHID, then couldn't open it, and reported nothing useful. Installing an editor alone would have hit the identical wall.

Two things landed:

1. **`system/etc/udev/rules.d/92-vial.rules`** — installed to `/etc/` and reloaded. Matches the vial magic serial (`vial:f64c2b3c`) rather than VID/PID, so it covers any Vial board.
2. **`pkgs.vial`** in `home.nix` — `home-manager switch --flake .#utsuho` applied clean.

I ran only the narrow install, not `mise run system:deploy` — that script also restarts oomd and nftables and masks keyring units, which you didn't ask for.

**Worth knowing:** upstream's rule uses `GROUP="users"`, which would be a no-op — you're not in `users`. And I verified `TAG+="uaccess"` produced **no ACL** on this host (`getfacl` shows no `user:sauyon` entry), consistent with the systemd-homed seat issue already documented in `home.nix`. So `GROUP="input"` is doing the real work, not redundancy.

**Evidence, end to end:**
```
hidraw12-15  crw-rw---- root input     (was crw------- root root)
open O_RDWR as sauyon .............. OK on all four
Vial raw HID (usage page 0xFF60) ... hidraw13
VIA protocol version ............... 9
Vial protocol / uid ................ 6 / 0x4829f621f27d181b
```
That uid matches the `uid` field in both `.vil` files — so the keymap I generated is for this exact board.

---

**Your call: the push is blocked, and it isn't my conflict.**

`master` diverged. A parallel session made 5 commits on the remote (drovr pin bumps, deleting `system/etc/nftables.d/drovr.nft` and `drovr-firewall.service`, trimming `system/deploy`). Local has 3 commits of mine plus 2 that aren't mine.

Dry-run merge says:
```
home.nix   auto-merges clean
flake.lock CONFLICT
```

The `flake.lock` conflict is between that session's local commits and the remote — **none of my commits touch `flake.lock`**. Resolving it means picking which drovr pin wins, and per your parallel-session rule I'm not guessing at that.

My three commits, waiting:
```
dda3c03 vial: install the editor and the udev rule it needs to see the keyboard
24cfdc0 svalboard: restore backtick, guard against orphaned keycodes
43bd65f svalboard: Hands Down Neu + Arensito symbols keymap
```

Tell me which drovr pin you want and I'll rebase and push, or take it yourself with `git pull --rebase origin master`.

Two smaller things still open: `/code-review` hasn't seen the udev rule or the `home.nix` change; and the unstaged `D .opencode/plugins/entire.ts` is still untouched.

content.text:
Vial won't launch from this shell, and I'm not going to work around it the way that would work.

**Cause:** Vial's bundled PyQt5 ships no Wayland plugin — only `libqxcb.so` — so it must go through XWayland. XWayland is up (`/tmp/.X11-unix/X0`) and rejects us:

```
Authorization required, but no authorization protocol specified
qt.qpa.screen: QXcbConnection: Could not connect to display :0
```

No X cookie exists to hand it. `XAUTHORITY` is unset in your systemd user environment (which does carry `DISPLAY=:0` and `WAYLAND_DISPLAY=wayland-1`), and there's no xauth file under `/run/user/60006`, in `~`, or in Hyprland's runtime dir. Hyprland's log has no XWayland or xauth lines at all.

The fix that would work from here is `xhost +local:`, which disables X access control for every local process for the rest of your session. That's a security change to your running desktop and it's your call, not mine — so I stopped.

**Next action: launch `Vial` from inside your Hyprland session** — your app launcher, or any terminal running in the session. The env is already correct there; this shell just isn't part of that session.

Both launch attempts exited on their own; nothing is left running.

```
hidraw12-15 .............. crw-rw---- root input   (was root-only)
open O_RDWR as sauyon .... OK on all four
Vial raw HID ............. hidraw13 (usage page 0xFF60)
VIA protocol ............. 9
Vial protocol / uid ...... 6 / 0x4829f621f27d181b  → matches both .vil files
```

So the permissions problem that broke browser KeyBard is genuinely fixed, and the keyboard answers the Vial protocol as you. When Vial opens it will see the board.

Tell me if you want `xhost +local:` and I'll run it — it'd let me launch Vial from here, at the cost of local X access control until your next login.

**KeyBard is open in Chromium now.** Click Connect, then load `~/devel/dotfiles/keyboards/svalboard/SvalHandsDownNeu.vil`.

```

```

**Vial can't run on this box right now, and it's not Vial's fault.** `xdpyinfo` — a plain X client with no bubblewrap — fails identically:

```
Authorization required, but no authorization protocol specified
unable to open display ":0"
```

Your Hyprland session started **Aug 17** and its Xwayland came up with no auth file:
```
Xwayland :0 -rootless -core -listenfd 57 -listenfd 58 -displayfd 128 -wm 125
                    ↑ no -auth
```
`XAUTHORITY` is unset in Hyprland's own environment and no cookie file exists anywhere. Xwayland reads its auth file only at startup, so this is unfixable on a running server — **every X11 app on this machine is broken until the compositor restarts**, not just Vial. Chromium is Wayland-native, which is why it sidesteps it.

Also worth knowing: the running compositor is **0.56.0**, the installed binary is **0.56.2**. The session is a version behind.

**I am not going to suggest you just log out.** Your own notes document that a passwordless login before the homed LUKS home unlocks starts `systemd --user` with `HOME=/`, which makes every home-manager user unit invisible for the whole boot — no waybar, no kanshi — and breaks `home-manager switch` at `Activating sops-nix`. A relogin is exactly the operation that triggers it, and the tailscaled patch that fixes it is built but **not deployed**. That's your call to make with eyes open, not a throwaway suggestion from me.

Three options, in the order I'd take them:

1. **Use KeyBard in Chromium** — open now, no restart, no risk. Does everything Vial does.
2. **Run Vial nested** — `cage 0.3.1` and `xwayland-satellite 0.8.2` are both in nixpkgs and would give Vial its own working Xwayland without touching your session. Say the word and I'll wire one up.
3. **Restart the session** — fixes X11 generally and picks up 0.56.2, but carries the homed risk above. Worth doing deliberately, ideally after deploying that tailscaled patch.

The udev fix is doing its job either way — that's what unblocked KeyBard, which failed for you originally purely on permissions.
